newsitem.title: USA: NetGrocer Inc joins online shopping business.
newsitem.headline: NetGrocer Inc joins online shopping business.

text.p: NetGrocer Inc will launch on Monday a new online grocery store that delivers canned food, toilet paper and other nonperishables for a small charge, in a bid to revolutionize the distribution of many store-bought items.

The Web-based service has no membership fee, but charges $2.99 to deliver, though Federal Express, ten pounds of its products anywhere in the country in a matter of days. It charges $0.99 for each additional ten pounds.
Daniel Nissan, president and chief executive of the company, said NetGrocer expects to make money in a manner similar to a traditional grocery store.

"We're targeting customers who want merchandise delivered to their homes without the hassle associated with supermarkets -- time spent on the trip, waiting in long lines and transporting heavy bags of groceries," Nissan said.
NetGrocer will buy its products from manufacturers, and then resell them to online shoppers for more than it paid.
It also hopes to eventually make money from manufacuters who will pay to NetGrocer to advertise and promote its products.
During the past eight weeks, NetGrocer has been in a trial phase with customers it attracted by advertising on various Internet sites.
Nissan said the service's most successful market was in Florida, where it was particularly popular with elderly and disabled customers.
NetGrocer, of course, is not the only company in the online grocery business. Analysts said the dominant company in the emerging industry is Peapod Inc, which went public last month.

Bruce Guptill, electronic commerce analyst at market research firm Gartner Group, said NetGrocer probably won't touch Peapod's customer base of 50,000 online shoppers for at least six months to a year.
Peapod sells perishable foods in major urban areas like Boston and Chicago, and it delivers it the same day.
Eventually, however, Guptill and other other analysts said NetGrocer could attract potential Peapod customers who discover the Web site.
"There's not a lot of pent-up demand for online grocery shopping right now," Guptill said.
Nissan, the company's founder, was formally a marketing executive at Vocaltec Inc , a developer of Internet communications software that allows callers to place phone calls via the Internet.
